overview.description: Nijū-kyū (Twenty-Nine) is a tactical Japanese card game focused on cumulative addition and card capture. Played with a standard deck, the objective is to be the player who plays a card that brings the total on the table exactly to twenty-nine. The player who hits the target 'sweeps' the table and collects the cards as scoring points. It is a game of subtraction-logic, card counting, and opportunistic 'sniping' of the target total.
overview.originName: 二十九 (にじゅうきゅう)

history.origins: Dates back to the mid-20th century, likely as a simplified variant of the Persian game 'Nard' or the Indian '29', but adapted into a 'Running Total' capture game for casual play in Japan.
timeline: 1950s: First documented in Japanese 'Trumps' (card game) manuals.
1980s: Becomes a popular educational game for teaching mental addition in elementary schools.
Present: Still played in social settings as a fast-paced filler game.
21st Century: Often found in Japanese 'Zasso' (miscellaneous) game collections.
history.evolution: Shifted from a betting-heavy game into a point-counting 'sweep' game.
history.cultural: Known for the satisfying 'Ching' or 'Sweep' moment when a player hits 29 and clears the table.

setup.dealing: All cards are dealt out equally to the players.

rules.objective: Capture the most cards by hitting the cumulative total of 29.
rules.gameplay:
1. Players take turns playing one card face-up to the table.
2. The total sum of point values is announced.
3. **Hitting 29**: If your card makes the total exactly 29, you win all cards on the table and keep them in your score pile.
4. **Passing**: If you only have cards that would push the total OVER 29, you must pass your turn.
5. **Reset**: After a sweep (hitting 29), the next player starts a new pile from zero.
keyRules: Card values: 2-10 equal face value; A, J, Q, K count as 1 point each.
Playing a card that makes the running total exactly 29 sweeps all table cards to your score pile.
If you have no card that can be played without exceeding 29, you must pass.
After a sweep, the next player starts a new pile from zero.

strategy.basic: Keep your 1-point cards (Aces and Face cards) for the final push. If the total is at 28, a Face card is a guaranteed win. Don't play your '10s' when the total is high (over 20), as you will almost certainly overshoot the 29 limit and be forced to pass.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Seven-Point Barrier': Many players hoard 7s and 8s. If you see an opponent play a low card (1 or 2) when the total is 20, they are likely trying to set up a '29' for their next turn. If you have a high card that takes it to 27 or 28, you 'pass' the opportunity to themâ€”sometimes it is better to play a 1 and take it to 21, forcing THEM to do the work.
strategy.advanced: Card Counting: There are exactly 4 cards of each rank. If all four 9-cards have been played, you know that a total of 20 is 'safe' from a single-card sweep by anyone holding a 9. Use this information to safely play your higher cards without gifting a sweep to the next player.
tips: In a 4-player game, teamwork isn't allowed, but you can intentionally 'set up' the player after you if you are far behind and want to stop the leader from winning a sweep.
If the total is at 25, only a 4-card or four 1s can win. Check your hand for these specific outs.

variations.noVariationsReason: Sources describe only the standard form; no regional or rule variations documented for Nijū-kyū.

difficulty.easy: Overplays high cards; doesn't save 1-point cards for the sweep; hits 'Pass' too often.
difficulty.hard: Expert at 'Setup Manipulation'; perfectly times the 29-sweep; master of the 'Process of Elimination' for opponent hands.
